# Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail: Company Statements, Audit Uncertainty, Missing Cash, Supervisory Failure, and Jan Marsalek

## Executive assessment

The evidence supplied supports a clear reconstruction of Wirecard’s public-fraud trail, but only within defined limits. The record shows a progression from repeated external warnings, through increasingly reassuring Wirecard communications, to a failed forensic verification of major revenues and escrow balances, followed by the discovery that approximately €1.9 billion in purported trust-account cash probably did not exist and Wirecard’s insolvency filing. The evidence also supports the assessment that Wirecard’s internal controls, supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting enforcement system, and market supervisor each failed in different ways.

The strongest conclusion is not merely that Wirecard’s public statements were later contradicted by events. It is that the company publicly presented KPMG’s investigation as broadly reassuring before the final report was available, while the final report could not verify central parts of the business and expressly identified serious evidentiary limitations. The supplied material therefore supports a finding of materially misleading public framing, although it does not, by itself, establish the criminal liability of any particular executive.

The supplied evidence does **not** establish a factual account of Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Although the requested investigation identifies Marsalek as a target, neither the Wirecard announcement nor the European Parliament study excerpt provides evidence about his disappearance, whereabouts, escape, associates, or legal status. Those matters must therefore be marked as **unsupported by the supplied sources**, rather than reconstructed speculatively.

## Sources and evidentiary method

Two source records are available:

1. A Wirecard/DGAP regulatory announcement dated April 28, 2020, reporting receipt of the KPMG special-investigation report and summarizing Wirecard’s interpretation of it. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))
2. A November 2020 European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit study, based on public information and cited underlying materials, which evaluates the Wirecard scandal and reconstructs a chronology through the company’s June 2020 insolvency filing. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The second source is an analytical policy study rather than a judicial finding. It repeatedly cautions against hindsight bias and distinguishes public allegations from established facts. Its account is nevertheless significant because it consolidates the chronology, describes institutional responsibilities, and identifies the evidentiary weaknesses in the oversight system.

## Chronology of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and critical information

The supplied study reports that concerns about Wirecard predated the final collapse by many years. In 2008, the shareholder association SdK allegedly questioned Wirecard’s unusually high margins and the treatment of customer deposits as company cash. The study further reports that EY was engaged to conduct a special audit of Wirecard’s 2007 accounts and subsequently became Wirecard’s group auditor. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study also identifies the 2016 Zatarra report, prepared by anonymous investors and associated with Matthew Earl and Fraser Perring, as alleging corruption, fraud, and money laundering. These were allegations, not adjudicated findings. The study notes that criminal proceedings connected with the Zatarra report were later discontinued after payment of a five-digit euro amount and were regarded as a minor market-manipulation case. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

From 2015 onward, Financial Times reporting described alleged inconsistencies in Wirecard’s accounts. In October 2018, employees connected with Wirecard’s Singapore operations reportedly supplied internal documents to Financial Times journalists because they believed an internal investigation had been suppressed. The identities of those whistleblowers were not publicly disclosed in the supplied material. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

These events are important because they establish that the eventual collapse did not arise without warning. The evidence instead indicates a long-running information trail involving analysts, short sellers, journalists, and alleged internal whistleblowers.

### 2019: regulatory intervention and the short-selling ban

On January 30, 2019, the Financial Times reportedly published an article alleging that Wirecard executives had used forged and backdated contracts to increase revenues. On February 15, BaFin directed Germany’s Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or FREP, to examine Wirecard’s interim accounts as of June 30, 2018. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

On February 18, BaFin prohibited the establishment or increase of net short positions in Wirecard shares until April 18, 2019. ESMA approved the measure. The policy study assesses this intervention critically, arguing that a short-selling ban can suppress negative information and delay the incorporation of adverse information into market prices. It also notes that some investors could have interpreted the ban as an indication that the regulator believed the short sellers were wrong. This is an assessment by the study’s authors, not a proven causal finding. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In April 2019, BaFin reportedly filed a criminal complaint against Financial Times journalists and ten short sellers on suspicion of market manipulation. The study records that BaFin also fined Wirecard €1.52 million for delayed publication of 2018 interim financial statements. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In October 2019, Wirecard hired KPMG to conduct an independent forensic investigation intended to address accusations published in the press and online. The engagement was therefore initiated by Wirecard itself, a fact relevant to the later public presentation of its results. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Wirecard’s public statements and the KPMG investigation

### The April 22 interim message

The supplied Wirecard source is associated with an April 22 webpage, but the text reproduced in the record is a regulatory announcement dated April 28. This is a source-format inconsistency that should not be silently ignored. The announcement states that the KPMG review had been extended until April 27 and that, “so far,” it had provided no evidence of balance-sheet manipulation. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The earlier public framing was reassuring. The announcement stated that the review covered four areas: third-party acquiring, merchant cash advance and digital lending, and business activities in India and Singapore. It claimed that no significant findings had been identified that would require adjustments to the 2016–2018 annual accounts. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

Wirecard also stated that existing audit documentation and procedures had been sufficient to prove third-party-acquiring revenues for 2016–2018. At the same time, however, it acknowledged that KPMG’s heightened forensic requirements had not been satisfied because relevant data were primarily controlled by third parties. Wirecard said it had supplied more than 200 million data records relating to December 2019 and that KPMG had found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances in that dataset. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

This distinction is critical. A clean result for a December 2019 dataset did not necessarily validate the disputed 2016–2018 third-party-acquiring revenues or the existence of historical escrow balances. The company’s statement placed emphasis on the absence of an identified adjustment while simultaneously acknowledging limitations in the underlying evidence.

### The April 28 KPMG report and evidentiary uncertainty

The Wirecard announcement states that KPMG delivered its report in the early hours of April 28. It repeats that incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had not been identified and that no significant findings required adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The European Parliament study presents a materially more cautious description of the report. It states that KPMG was unable to verify approximately €1 billion in foreign trust accounts because of insufficient documentation by Wirecard and its third-party acquirers. It further states that KPMG could neither refute nor confirm the allegations and urged further investigation. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study also quotes KPMG as being unable to state whether the relevant TPA revenues existed and were correct in amount, or whether they did not exist and were incorrect. That is not an exonerating conclusion. It is an unresolved evidentiary conclusion. The inability to verify a material asset or revenue stream does not itself prove fraud, but it directly undermines any broad claim that the investigation had validated Wirecard’s historical accounts. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Missing cash and the collapse of the company’s position

The chronology changes sharply in June 2020. On June 18, BaFin reportedly filed a criminal complaint against Wirecard concerning accounting fraud and potentially market manipulation through incorrect disclosures in the 2016–2018 annual financial statements. On June 22, Wirecard’s board stated that the €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist and that the third-party business might be incorrect in the manner previously described. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

On June 25, Wirecard filed for insolvency because of impending insolvency and over-indebtedness. The study reports that EY then described “clear indications” of a sophisticated fraud involving multiple parties and stated that bank confirmations concerning certain escrow accounts were forged. EY refused to sign off on the 2019 accounts. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The most defensible interpretation is that the disappearance of the purported €1.9 billion was not merely an ordinary accounting classification dispute. It represented a fundamental failure of cash verification and called into question the reliability of previously published financial statements. However, the supplied sources do not establish the complete mechanism by which the alleged false balances were created, who directed it, or where any money may have gone.

## Supervisory and audit failures

### External audit

The European Parliament study states that EY issued unqualified opinions on Wirecard’s 2015–2017 financial statements and again for 2018, despite public allegations concerning the company. The study reports that KPMG could not verify the existence of the escrow accounts and questioned whether they were appropriately classified as cash or cash equivalents under IFRS. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study also reports allegations that EY relied on confirmations issued in the name of a trustee rather than independently confirming the balances directly with the relevant banks. These are reported allegations and should not be treated as a final adjudication of EY’s legal liability. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The authors’ assessment is that the audit system failed to provide adequate assurance against material misstatement and fraud. They recommend stronger auditor liability, greater disclosure about audit-firm inspection findings, and a clearer legal requirement for professional skepticism and reasonable checks for accounting manipulation. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### FREP and BaFin

Before 2022 reforms, Germany used a two-step financial-reporting enforcement system in which FREP performed the first stage and BaFin acted in specified circumstances. The study argues that FREP depended heavily on company cooperation and lacked statutory investigative powers. It characterizes the division of authority as creating latency and unclear responsibility. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study reports that FREP’s earlier random checks of Wirecard accounts did not identify reporting errors. After the 2019 Financial Times reports, BaFin directed FREP to investigate, but the process did not result in the discovery of the missing €1.9 billion before the company’s collapse. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The authors’ broader conclusion is that all five defensive lines failed in some respect: internal controls, the supervisory board, external audit, financial-reporting and audit oversight, and BaFin. This is an institutional assessment, not a finding that every participant acted unlawfully. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek: evidentiary limits

The supplied evidence contains no substantive information about Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. It does not identify a date, location, travel route, alleged assistance, current whereabouts, or judicial finding concerning him. It also does not provide a source-supported relationship between Marsalek and the missing €1.9 billion.

Accordingly, the public-fraud trail reconstructed here cannot validly extend from Wirecard’s collapse to Marsalek’s disappearance. Any narrative connecting him to the disappearance, alleged flight, intelligence networks, or the mechanics of the missing cash would require additional sources not included in the benchmark material. The appropriate conclusion is therefore **not proven from the supplied evidence**, rather than an inference based on his senior position or public prominence.

## Contradictions and unresolved tensions

| Issue | Company presentation | Other supplied evidence | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| KPMG findings | No incriminating evidence and no required account adjustments | KPMG could not verify approximately €1 billion and could neither confirm nor refute key revenue allegations | The statements are not necessarily logically identical, but the company’s presentation was materially more reassuring than the evidentiary limitations described by the study. |
| Third-party-acquiring revenues | Existing audit measures were sufficient to prove revenues | KPMG reportedly could not determine whether relevant revenues existed or were correct in amount | Direct evidentiary tension. |
| Trust-account cash | No immediate adjustment identified | About €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist by June 22 | Later facts fundamentally undermined confidence in the reported cash. |
| Source date | URL refers to April 22 | Reproduced announcement is dated April 28 | Metadata/date inconsistency in the supplied record. |
| Jan Marsalek disappearance | No information | No information | Unsupported subject; no conclusion warranted. |

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a firm, evidence-based opinion: Wirecard’s public-fraud trail was characterized by years of warnings, weak challenge from oversight institutions, reassuring corporate messaging, unresolved forensic evidence, and the eventual collapse of a central cash representation. The April 2020 Wirecard announcement should not be read as confirmation that the historical accounts had been independently validated. The more cautious interpretation is that KPMG had not proven fraud in every investigated area, but also had not verified key revenues and assets.

The supervisory failure was systemic. It involved not only the company’s management but also internal governance, external audit, financial-reporting enforcement, and BaFin’s handling of adverse information. Nevertheless, the supplied sources do not justify assigning criminal responsibility to specific individuals or explaining Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. Those issues remain outside the evidentiary boundaries of this record.

(2020, November). *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?* Economic Governance Support Unit, Directorate-General for Internal Policies, European Parliament.
